system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-07-03 16:44:00 to 2179-07-07 20:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient, status post orthotopic liver transplant, was admitted for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes and new-onset tremors. A liver biopsy was performed, which ruled out rejection but showed neutrophilic inflammation. An ERCP revealed a biliary stricture at the anastomosis, which was treated with sphincterotomy and placement of two biliary stents. His liver function tests subsequently improved. He developed hyperkalemia, managed with kayexalate, fludrocortisone, and low-dose furosemide. Neurological evaluation for abnormal involuntary movements, including head shaking and facial grimacing, found no acute intracranial or spinal cord abnormalities on MRI; the movements resolved, and a psychological component was considered. An EGD showed only mild gastropathy. The patient stabilized, resumed oral intake, and was discharged home with family support, visiting nurse services, and a plan for weekly lab monitoring.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of prostate

Discharge Instructions:
Please call the Transplant Office ___ if you have any 
of the following: 
-fever (101 or greater), chills, nausea, vomiting, increased 
abdominal pain or distension, constipation, pain/burning/urgency 
with urination or incision redness/bleeding/drainage
-You may shower
-No driving while taking pain medication
-No heavy lifting (nothing heavier than 10 pounds)or straining
-Please be sure to continue your tube feeding for at least 20 
hours daily and we encourage you to eat food by mouth as much as 
possible. 
-If tube feeding stopped for any reason, be sure to flush tube 
with 30cc of water to prevent clogging of tube.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Status post liver transplant with abdominal pain.

Comparison radiograph available from ___.

SUPINE AND UPRIGHT FRONTAL ABDOMINAL RADIOGRAPHS:  Two plastic biliary stents
are redemonstrated, unchanged in position since the ___, exam. 
Patient is status post cholecystectomy.  A non-obstructive bowel gas pattern
is present.  No free air is detected.  Multiple intrapelvic surgical clips are
unchanged in position.

INDICATION:  The patient is a ___ male status post liver
transplantation with worsening epigastric pain.  Evaluate for acute process.

EXAMINATION:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.

COMPARISONS:  ___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Helically acquired axial images were obtained from the lung bases
to the pubic symphysis after the uneventful administration of oral and 100 mL
of Visipaque intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformations are
provided for review.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:
The lung bases are clear with no focal consolidations, pulmonary nodules or
pleural effusions.  There is bibasilar atelectasis.

The patient is status post liver transplantation.  In the interim, there has
been placement of a biliary stent extending into the hepatic hilum.  There is
associated pneumobilia.  There is no new intra- or extra-hepatic biliary
dilatation.  There are no new focal liver lesions.  Noted on the previous
examination immediately superior to the anastomotic site, there is focal
hypodensity seen within the inferior vena cava, which may be representative of
an area of focal thrombus.  The spleen, partially atrophied pancreas, both
adrenal glands, both kidneys, both ureters are unremarkable.  Located in the
region of the duodenal bulb (series 2A:Image 24), there is an area of focal
fluid, that is felt most likely to be intraluminal measuring 12.1 x 1.6 cm. 
There has been essential resolution of previously noted areas of fluid
demonstrated from ___.  The visualized portions of intra-abdominal
small and large bowel are unremarkable. There is no intra-abdominal free air
or free fluid.  There is no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The rectum, sigmoid colon,
bladder, prostate and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.  The patient is
status post penile prosthesis placement, with the reservoir demonstrated
within the left inguinal region.  There is no pelvic-free fluid.  There is no
pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

BONE WINDOWS:  The visualized osseous structures are unremarkable and no
suspicious lytic or sclerotic foci.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No definite acute intra-abdominal process.  Essential resolution of
previously noted areas of fluid from ___.

2.  Focal area of fluid in the region of the duodenal bulb, felt most likely
to be intraluminal, small collection immediately adjacent and compressing in
the duodenum is felt less likely.  

3.  Focal hypodensity in the inferior vena cava as previously noted
immediately superior to the anastomosis site, may represent focal thrombosis.

INDICATION:  Feeding tube for failure to thrive

NASOINTESTINAL TUBE REPOSITIONING:  The existing nasointestinal tube is seen
with the appropriate position with the tip in the stomach.  The right naris
was anesthetized with lidocaine jelly and the throat with hurricane spray. 
Under fluoroscopic guidance, the Dobbhoff tube was advanced until the tip
reached the third part of the duodenum.  Tube position was confirmed with a 20
mL injection of Optiray.

IMPRESSION:  Successful repositioning of the Dobbhoff tube into the
post-pyloric position.  The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your care team doctors. I understand you've been having some trouble eating since your last discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. Every time I try to eat, my stomach starts to ache, especially around the belly button area. I just don’t feel like eating at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it started about 10 days ago, after your last hospital stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I was doing okay at first, but then the pain came back, and I’ve lost my appetite. I also noticed looser stools lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. You’re not having nausea, vomiting, fevers, or jaundice, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. Just the stomach ache and not feeling hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history with the liver transplant and the biliary stent, we want to make sure nothing’s blocking or irritating your digestive tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. But I’m worried—could this be another stricture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with a CT scan today, and the biliary stents are still in place and unchanged. No signs of new blockage or free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good to hear. What about that fluid they mentioned near my duodenum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT did show a small area of fluid near the duodenal bulb, but it looks like it’s inside the bowel, not a collection pressing on it. It’s likely not the main cause of your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you're not getting enough nutrition because of the pain when you eat. The team is concerned about 'failure to thrive.' We’d like to place a feeding tube to help you get proper nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A feeding tube? Through the nose again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a Dobhoff tube. We’ll place it past your stomach, into the small intestine—post-pyloric—so it bypasses the area that might be sensitive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb your nose and throat. You might feel some pressure, but it shouldn’t be painful. It’s done under X-ray guidance to make sure it’s placed correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you. Let’s do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The tube was placed successfully yesterday under fluoroscopy. It’s now in the correct position in your duodenum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, already? I didn’t feel much. Is it working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we started tube feeds this morning. You’re getting Isosource 1.5 cal at 55 ml per hour. Nutrition says you’re tolerating it well—no nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still have that right-sided pain—hip, groin, sometimes flank. It comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we reviewed that. The CT showed a small right inguinal hernia, but your pain isn’t always there. Urology checked and said it’s not related to your penile implant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chronic pain service thinks it’s neuropathic or musculoskeletal. They recommended a Lidoderm patch for the right hip area and increasing gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been on gabapentin before. Isn’t that hard on the liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We actually decided to stop gabapentin to avoid too many medications. Instead, we’re starting nortriptyline at night—it helps with both nerve pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having trouble sleeping too. Maybe that will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Geriatrics also recommended increasing your mirtazapine from 7.5 to 15 mg at bedtime. It can help with both appetite and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. But I’m still worried about my stomach. Why does it hurt when I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to your history of esophageal dysmotility and hiatal hernia. The tube feeds bypass the stomach, so we can give your GI tract a rest while you get nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 1.4, down from 1.6—your kidneys are doing better. Liver enzymes are slightly up but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any word on the infection test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination from skin or genital area. No sign of real infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Phew. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The pain is improving, especially with the nortriptyline. You’re walking more, and the Lidoderm patch seems to help the hip pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s not gone, but it’s better when I move around. I even tried a little food yesterday—no pain, but I didn’t eat much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We want you to keep using the tube feed for at least 20 hours a day for now. We’ll recheck in clinic and maybe adjust later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I noticed a change in my CellCept.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we switched from mycophenolate mofetil (CellCept) to Myfortic. It’s the same family but easier on the stomach. We made sure your pharmacy has it before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I had a lot of stomach issues with the old one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re getting ready to discharge you. You’re alert, walking independently, pain is manageable, and you’re tolerating the tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I want to make sure I do this right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Keep the tube feeding going—20 hours a day. Flush the tube with 30 cc of water if it stops or before and after meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the transplant office if you have fever over 101, vomiting, severe pain, or issues with the incision. No driving while on tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the Lidoderm patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One patch daily on the painful area—on for 12 hours, off for 12. And keep taking the new mirtazapine and nortriptyline at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. We’ll see you in follow-up. Keep building your strength and keep in touch.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient, status post liver transplant with a history of biliary stricture treated with stent placement, was readmitted 10 days after discharge for failure to thrive and postprandial abdominal pain. He reported decreased oral intake, early satiety, and intermittent supraumbilical discomfort. Imaging confirmed stable biliary stents and no acute abdominal process, though a small fluid area near the duodenum was noted. A post-pyloric Dobhoff tube was placed under fluoroscopic guidance, and enteral feeding was initiated successfully. Chronic right-sided pain, possibly neuropathic, improved with nortriptyline and a Lidoderm patch, while gabapentin was discontinued to reduce polypharmacy. Depression and insomnia were addressed with an increased dose of mirtazapine. Myfortic replaced mycophenolate mofetil due to gastrointestinal side effects. The patient stabilized, tolerated tube feeds, and was discharged home with instructions for ongoing nutrition, medication management, and follow-up.
